power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: HC participants were excluded if they had a history of substance dependence, a current or past Axis I disorder, or a first-degree relative with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia.

Exclusion criteria for all participants included head trauma with loss of consciousness lasting more than 5 minutes, a history of seizures or electroconvulsive therapy, neurological disorders, and a positive urine drug screen.
Demographic, clinical, and cognitive characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1.
Following the diagnostic interviews and mood symptom assessments described above, all participants completed two behavioral tasks (Fig. 1) and several self-report measures relevant to BD.

Participants completed two probabilistic learning tasks characterized by distinct sources and patterns of contingency change (i.e., reversals): a probability-tracking task (PTT; Behrens et al., 2007) with predetermined contingency changes across stable and volatile phases and a probabilistic reversal learning task (PRL; Hampton et al., 2006) with performance-contingent reversals.
Participants completed two or three blocks, with each block consisting of 200 trials.
Phase order was counterbalanced across participants, and each participant completed one block of 300 trials.

text.text: Bipolar disorder (BD) is marked by extreme mood fluctuations, yet the computational mechanisms underlying this instability remain poorly understood.
Recent computational accounts suggest that mood instability may arise from altered reward prediction error (RPE) processing, yet little is known about the factors that modulate this process.
Volatility inference-the ability to track environmental change-may be particularly relevant as it modulates the influence of prediction errors on belief updating.
However, it remains unclear whether BD is characterized by altered volatility inference.
We investigated whether BD showed altered volatility inference across distinct environmental structures using decision-making tasks and computational modeling.

Individuals with bipolar I disorder (BD-I; N = 32) and healthy controls (HC; N = 40) completed two tasks: a probabilitytracking task (PTT) with predetermined contingency changes across stable and volatile phases and a probabilistic reversal learning task (PRL) with performance-contingent reversals.
The BD-I group showed reduced performance and switched choices more frequently than the HC group across both tasks.

Computational modeling further revealed heightened volatility beliefs in the BD-I group, reflected by a higher prior belief about volatility in the PTT and higher tonic volatility in the PRL, together with greater behavioral stochasticity across both tasks.
These computational alterations were not associated with current manic or depressive symptom severity.

These findings suggest that BD-I shows deficits in adapting to volatile environments, potentially arising from trait-like computational alterations characterized by heightened expectations of environmental change and noisy belief-to-action mapping, which may provide candidate mechanisms through which decision-making abnormalities contribute to mood instability.
Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic mood disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of mania and depression (Grande et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic mood disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of mania and depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Grande et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Despite mood instability being a central symptom in BD, the mechanisms underlying these extreme mood fluctuations remain poorly understood.

BD has also been widely associated with abnormalities across multiple facets of reward-based decision making, including altered reward sensitivity, reward learning and adaptation to changing reward contingencies (Johnson et al., 2012; Whitton et al., 2015; Long et al., 2022).

text.text: In light of recent computational accounts of mood, such alterations in decision making may provide valuable insights for understanding the mechanisms underlying mood instability in BD.

Recent computational accounts have suggested that mood is shaped not simply by objective outcomes, but by the discrepancy between prior expectations and experienced outcomes, as captured by reward prediction errors (Rutledge et al., 2014 (Rutledge et al., , 2015)).

text.text: This perspective highlights a close link between mood and decision-making processes, whereby iterative learning shapes expectations and choices influence the subsequent outcomes individuals experience, ultimately shaping mood dynamics (Eldar et al., 2016; Blain and Rutledge, 2020).

text.text: Building on this computational view of mood, frameworks that model decision-making processes to identify the generative processes underlying mood have emerged as a promising avenue for developing mechanistic accounts of mood disturbances in affective disorders, including BD (Mason et al., 2017; Zavlis et al., 2026).

text.text: Computational studies in BD have identified disruptions in decision-making processes, including noisy belief-to-action mapping (Yechiam et al., 2008; Lasagna et al., 2022; MacDonald et al., 2025) and abnormalities in reward prediction error (RPE) processing or belief updating (Ossola et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2024).

text.text: Moreover, beyond simply identifying such alterations in BD, recent work has suggested that disruptions in these processes may be related to mood fluctuations.

Crucially, recent studies have proposed that the sum of recent RPEs, or environmental momentum, may reflect mood and bias subsequent reward perception, thereby altering future RPEs and forming a feedback loop between mood and reward processing, and amplification of this feedback process has been proposed as a computational mechanism underlying mood instability in BD (Eldar and Niv, 2015; Mason et al., 2017; Moningka and Mason, 2024).

text.text: These findings suggest that disruptions in reward-related decisionmaking processes may actually contribute to mood fluctuations, highlighting the importance of identifying which components of decision making are altered and relevant to mood dynamics in BD.
However, given the relatively early stage of computational approaches in BD, several potentially important components remain underexplored.
One such component is the inference of how rapidly the environment changes, commonly referred to as environmental volatility (Behrens et al., 2007).

text.text: Given the continually changing nature of the real-world environment, accurately tracking volatility is critical for adaptive behavior, and disruptions in this process have been implicated across a range of psychiatric conditions and symptoms including psychosis (Deserno et al., 2020), anxiety (Hein et al., 2021) and borderline personality disorder (Henco et al., 2020).

text.text: Given that inferred volatility can shape expectations of the world by determining how strongly prediction errors influence belief updating (Nassar et al., 2010; Mathys et al., 2011 Mathys et al., , 2014) ) and that recent accounts propose that mood dynamics are shaped by prediction errors (Rutledge et al., 2014 (Rutledge et al., , 2015;; Eldar et al., 2016), altered volatility inference may therefore contribute to mood instability.

text.text: In line with this possibility, two recent studies using computational modeling of probabilistic reversal learning have investigated whether BD shows alterations in beliefs about environmental change, yet the findings are inconsistent. Ivanova et al. (2025) found higher prior and overall beliefs about environmental volatility in euthymic BD, whereas MacDonald et al. (2025) found no evidence that BD held elevated reversal beliefs that reward contingencies would reverse.

text.text: Despite these mixed findings in computational studies, consistent behavioral patterns observed in previous studies may provide indirect evidence for heightened volatility beliefs in BD.

Previous studies have reported impaired adaptation in BD, often accompanied by increased choice switching, when learning associations in probabilistic environments (Minassian et al., 2004; Pizzagalli et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2017; Urošević et al., 2018) or in environments where reward contingencies change over time (Roiser et al., 2009; Ivanova et al., 2025; MacDonald et al., 2025).

text.text: Given that elevated choice switching has been associated with heightened expectations of environmental change in humans (Schiffer et al., 2017; Deserno et al., 2020), these behavioral patterns may provide indirect support for the possibility that BD is characterized by overestimated environmental volatility.

text.text: However, this interpretation remains partly speculative, as most previous studies did not computationally dissociate the potential underlying mechanisms.

Specifically, it remains unclear whether this heightened switching behavior arises from overestimated environmental volatility or reflects greater noise in belief-to-action mapping as reported by MacDonald et al. (2025), or both.

text.text: Nonetheless, findings that individuals with BD show greater sensitivity to recent feedback, particularly when it conflicts with prior reinforcement history (Pizzagalli et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2017), may suggest that elevated behavioral variability may not be fully explained by choice randomness.

text.text: Computational approaches are therefore needed to dissociate these two possibilities, enabling us to test whether such behavioral patterns could be explained by heightened volatility beliefs in BD.
Another crucial question is whether alterations in volatility inference vary with current mood symptoms of mania and depression.
However, few studies have directly examined associations between symptom severity and measures indicative of altered volatility inference, with most available evidence coming from euthymic samples.

For mania, greater residual manic symptoms were associated with lower uncertainty about reward contingencies in a changing environment (Ivanova et al., 2025), contrary to what would be expected under heightened volatility beliefs.

text.text: Taken together, the relationship between mood symptoms and volatility inference in BD remains unclear, which may be attributable to the scarcity of studies or the limited range of mood symptom severity in previous samples.

Here, we aimed to examine whether bipolar I disorder (BD-I) shows alterations in volatility inference using computational modeling across two well-established probabilistic learning tasks-a probability-tracking task (PTT) and a probabilistic reversal learning task (PRL)-which differ in the sources and patterns of environmental change.

By examining whether patterns of volatility inference and group differences are consistent across distinct environmental structures, we aimed to characterize these alterations more comprehensively while better reflecting the complexity of the real-world environment.

We hypothesized that BD would show reduced behavioral performance in both tasks, consistent with previous findings (Gorrindo et al., 2005; Roiser et al., 2009; Wegbreit et al., 2016; Ivanova et al., 2025; MacDonald et al., 2025), underpinned by heightened volatility beliefs, as reported in a previous study (Ivanova et al., 2025).

text.text: Participants completed two probabilistic learning tasks characterized by distinct sources and patterns of contingency change (i.e., reversals): a probability-tracking task (PTT; Behrens et al., 2007) with predetermined contingency changes across stable and volatile phases and a probabilistic reversal learning task (PRL; Hampton et al., 2006) with performance-contingent reversals.

text.text: In both tasks, participants repeatedly chose between two options that probabilistically yielded rewards, while they were informed that one option was more advantageous at any given time and that the relative advantage could reverse during the task.
Task order was counterbalanced across participants (see Supplementary Material for additional task details).
In the PRL, the chosen option could yield either a gain or a loss of 25 points.
The better option yielded gains with 80% probability and losses with 20% probability, with the opposite contingencies for the worse option.

Reversals were performance-contingent: after four consecutive selections of the better option, the reversal probability was 25% on each subsequent trial and increased to 100% after eight consecutive selections.
Participants completed two or three blocks, with each block consisting of 200 trials.
In the PTT, the options displayed the reward magnitude that could be earned, which varied across trials independently of the underlying reward contingency.

The task comprised a stable phase (120 trials) in which the reward contingency of the better option remained constant at 75% and a volatile phase (180 trials) in which the better option had an 80% reward contingency and its identity reversed every 30 or 40 trials at predetermined points.
Phase order was counterbalanced across participants, and each participant completed one block of 300 trials.

To characterize participants' trial-by-trial belief-updating processes, we used the Hierarchical Gaussian Filter for binary inputs (HGF; Mathys et al., 2011 Mathys et al., , 2014)), a well-established computational framework that describes how an agent learns about an uncertain quantity from binary inputs.

text.text: The HGF is a perceptual model that assumes that an agent has an internal generative model of the environment, represented by a hierarchy of environmental states 𝑥 (𝑘) , with k indexing trials.

For example, in the 3level HGF, the model is represented by a hierarchy of 𝑥 1 (𝑘) , 𝑥 2 (𝑘) and 𝑥 3 (𝑘) , where 𝑥 1 (𝑘) (level 1) represents the binary input, 𝑥 2 (𝑘) (level 2) represents the latent tendency toward a particular category (i.e., how likely option 1 is to yield a positive outcome on trial k), and 𝑥 3 (𝑘) (level 3) represents environmental log-volatility.

Beliefs about these states are represented by probability distributions, whose means (𝜇 1 , 𝜇 2 , 𝜇 3 ) reflect current belief estimates and whose variances (𝜎 1 , 𝜎 2 , 𝜎 3 ) reflect their uncertainty.

In the current tasks, 𝜇 1 corresponds to the probability that option 1 will be rewarding and is obtained by applying a sigmoid transformation to 𝜇 2 , which represents the latent tendency for option 1 to be rewarding; 𝜇 3 corresponds to phasic log-volatility, governing changes at the second level.

text.text: Task performance was defined separately for each task to reflect its specific characteristics.
In the PTT, task performance was assessed using accuracy, defined as the proportion of correct choices across trials.
In the PRL, task performance was assessed using reversal counts, defined as the number of reversals in each block.

text.text: The vertically arranged panels illustrate the hierarchical propagation of beliefs from environmental volatility to lower-level beliefs and decisions, showing how differences in HGF parameters lead to distinct belief-updating and decision-making trajectories under a similar environmental structure.

Compared with the HC participant, the BD participant showed higher prior and trial-wise volatility beliefs (A) and greater level-2 uncertainty (B), reflecting greater sensitivity to recent outcomes during belief updating.

In turn, this greater uncertainty led to greater fluctuations in lower-level beliefs (C), ultimately producing more frequent choice switching, visible as more frequent vertical transitions in the decision trajectories (D), while greater behavioral stochasticity also contributed to this switching pattern.

Our findings showed that BD-I exhibited reduced performance and elevated switching behavior, underpinned by computational signatures of heightened beliefs about environmental volatility and increased behavioral stochasticity in volatile environments.

By demonstrating that these alterations were consistent across two environments with distinct sources and patterns of environmental change, our study provides evidence that heightened volatility inference may characterize BD.
Moreover, the altered volatility belief was not associated with current manic or depressive symptoms.

Together, these findings suggest that BD shows deficits in adapting to a volatile environment, potentially arising from heightened expectations of environmental change and noisy belief-to-action mapping, which may represent trait-like rather than state-dependent characteristics varying with current mood symptoms.
Our findings replicated previously reported abnormalities in decision making in BD.

The impaired performance and elevated switching behavior observed in the current study are consistent with behavioral patterns previously reported among individuals with BD in uncertain environments (Minassian et al., 2004; Pizzagalli et al., 2008; Roiser et al., 2009; Ryu et al., 2017; Urošević et al., 2018; Ivanova et al., 2025; MacDonald et al., 2025).

Specifically, our findings suggested that computational alterations previously reported in BD, including greater behavioral stochasticity (Yechiam et al., 2008; Lasagna et al., 2022; MacDonald et al., 2025) and heightened beliefs about environmental volatility (Ivanova et al., 2025), may both contribute to these behavioral patterns.

text.text: Notably, whereas previous evidence regarding volatility inference in BD has been unclear, the present findings provide converging evidence for heightened volatility inference by demonstrating this pattern across two distinct environmental structures and in a sample with broader symptom variability, extending previous evidence from a euthymic sample examined in a single environment (Ivanova et al., 2025).

text.text: Together, the present study integrates previously disparate behavioral and computational findings while adding converging evidence for heightened volatility inference, a relatively underexplored computational alteration in BD, providing a more unified account of aberrant decision making in BD.

Beyond accounting for aberrant decision making, the current finding of heightened volatility inference may also provide a nuanced account of mood instability when integrated with previously proposed computational models of mood and BD.

Recent computational frameworks propose that mood reflects discrepancies between expectations and outcomes as captured by RPEs (Rutledge et al., 2014 (Rutledge et al., , 2015;; Blain and Rutledge, 2020).

text.text: By shaping expectations that deviate from the true states of the world, heightened volatility beliefs in BD may generate larger prediction errors and potentially contribute to mood fluctuations.

Furthermore, heightened volatility inference may influence mood by modulating the recursive interaction between environmental momentum and reward perception proposed in the momentum-bias model (Eldar and Niv, 2015).

text.text: According to the model, environmental momentum, formalized as a sum of recent RPEs and proposed to reflect mood state, can bias subsequent reward perception (i.e., reward is experienced as more or less rewarding when recent outcomes signal the environment is improving or deteriorating).

As this biased reward perception shapes subsequent RPEs, this process can form a recursive feedback loop, with greater momentum bias having previously been associated with hypomanic traits and BD (Eldar and Niv, 2015; Moningka and Mason, 2024).

text.text: Accordingly, heightened volatility beliefs in BD may increase sensitivity to recent RPEs, potentially strengthening the accumulation of recent RPEs into environmental momentum and thereby amplifying the feedback loop that may give rise to extreme mood fluctuations; however, this mechanistic link remains to be tested empirically.

Future studies could use designs that jointly measure volatility inference and environmental momentum to test whether volatility inference can be incorporated into the existing momentum-bias model of BD.
The current findings may have several clinical implications.

First, heightened volatility beliefs may provide a possible account of clinical phenomena observed in BD, such as why specific life events (e.g., goal-achievement or goal-striving) precede increases in manic symptoms (Johnson et al., 2008) or episode onset (Nusslock et al., 2007).

text.text: By increasing sensitivity to incoming evidence, heightened volatility beliefs may lead individuals with BD to interpret ordinary life events as overly salient signals of environmental change (e.g., the environment has become more favorable or opportunity-rich), thereby potentially facilitating manic symptoms or transitions into mood episodes.
Second, relationships between volatility inference and clinical characteristics may offer additional clinical insights.
In the current study, volatility inference did not vary with manic or depressive symptom severity.

Together with findings from a euthymic BD sample (Ivanova et al., 2025), our finding raises the possibility that heightened volatility inference may represent a trait-like characteristic of BD that can potentially serve as a computational marker, particularly in the differential diagnosis with unipolar depression.

text.text: The present finding may point to a computational process underlying heightened BAS sensitivity: heightened volatility beliefs may increase reward responsiveness by causing reward outcomes to be interpreted as more salient (i.e., signaling environmental change), although this possibility requires further investigation.
Although the current findings provide new insights into computational mechanisms underlying mood fluctuations in BD, several important questions remain.

First, it remains unclear whether heightened volatility inference develops over the course of BD, represents a pre-existing vulnerability, or both. Ivanova et al. Second, an important extension would be to examine whether altered volatility inference is specific to beliefs about the external environment or also extends to beliefs about internal states or self-beliefs.

Third, further work could directly test how elevated volatility beliefs relate to moment-to-moment mood dynamics, thereby evaluating our proposed account of how volatility beliefs may contribute to mood fluctuations.

One possible approach is to repeatedly sample momentary mood during a task and relate these reports to model-derived trial-wise estimates of volatility or uncertainty, leveraging paradigms from Blain and Rutledge (2020).

text.text: Furthermore, future studies could combine this laboratory-based approach with computational modeling of real-world mood dynamics.
Notably, Pulcu et al. (2022) identified elevated affective volatility as a prominent feature of real-world mood dynamics in BD.

text.text: Future studies could examine whether laboratory-derived computational parameters, such as elevated volatility beliefs identified in the present study, are associated with this real-world affective volatility and whether incorporating these parameters into models of mood dynamics could improve their predictive accuracy.
Finally, it should be noted that the present findings alone may not fully explain all aspects of mood dynamics in BD.
For example, although heightened volatility beliefs may help account for transitions into mood episodes, they may appear to contradict the persistence of mood within an episode.

If heightened volatility beliefs increase sensitivity to recent outcomes and promote belief updating, then why do mood and behavior remain rigid in BD despite the mood-incongruent evidence during episodes (i.e., the persistence of depressive mood despite success cues during a depressive episode or excessive goal-directed activity during mania despite failure cues)?

One possibility is that heightened volatility beliefs and within-episode mood rigidity are not mutually exclusive, with volatility inference operating in a mood-congruent manner such that the environment is inferred to be changing more rapidly when recent outcomes align with the current mood state.
For example, during mania, positive RPEs may be interpreted as stronger evidence that the environment is rapidly improving, whereas negative RPEs may be more salient in depression.

This could produce asymmetric, valence-dependent belief updating that preferentially amplifies evidence congruent with the ongoing mood episode while attenuating the influence of incongruent evidence, further shaping environmental momentum and thereby exaggerating biases in reward perception.

Future research should examine whether volatility inference varies across mood episodes and how it relates to the momentum-bias account, thereby contributing to a more integrative computational model of mood instability in BD that better captures clinically relevant phenomena.

We demonstrated that BD-I exhibited heightened beliefs about environmental volatility, accompanied by noisy belief-to-action mapping that may underlie impaired adaptation and elevated switching across dynamically changing environments.

These computational alterations did not vary with current manic or depressive symptom severity, suggesting that they may represent relatively stable characteristics rather than mood-dependent features.

Together, these findings contribute to the mechanistic understanding of aberrant decision making in BD by identifying computational alterations in both belief updating and action selection, proposing candidate mechanisms through which decisionmaking abnormalities may contribute to mood instability.
